title: On-going User
text:
There are a few ways to navigate GitHub for on-going use:

Create a new repository through GitHub – creating a new repository on the cloud
Clone a repository through GitHub Desktop – adding a repository that’s on the cloud onto your local computer
Create a new repository through GitHub Desktop – creating a new repository onto your local computer
Add an existing R project as new repository



1. Create a new repository on GitHub

Go to GitHub and make sure you’re logged in
Near “Repositories”, click New button
How to fill this in:

Repository template: No template
Repository name: desired repository name
Description: any information you want fellow users to know
Private
Initialize this repository with: Add a README file

Click Create repository button
Click <>Code button
Copy the HTTPS address



2. Clone a repository through GitHub Desktop

Click Current repository ▼
Click Add ▼
Click Clone a repository…

Now, there are 2 choices… you can either a) search through the existing repositories b) copy and paste the HTTPS address

In the GitHub.com tab:

select the existing repository
choose local path you’d like to save it to

In the URL tab:

select the existing repository
choose local path you’d like to save it to



Click Clone



3. Create a new repository through GitHub Desktop

Click Current repository ▼
Click Add ▼
Click Create a new repository..



How to fill this in:

Repository name: desired repository name
Description: any information you want fellow users to know
Local path: choose path you’d like to save it to
Initialize this repository with a README
Git ignore: ▼ scroll and select R
License: None
Click Create repository button


It will ask if you want to Publish repository, click Publish repository button


4. Add an existing R project as a new repository

Open your .Rproj file
At the top of your RStudio window, click “Tools”
Click “Version Control > Project setup…”
A new window “Project Options” window will open with “Git/SVN”tab displayed

Change Version control systems (None)▼ to Git


A pop up message:

Confirm Restart RStudio
You’ll need to restart RStudio in order for this change to take effect. Do you want to do this now?

Click “Yes”

Go to GitHub Desktop
Click Current repository ▼
At the bottom under Other, you’ll notice your project - click it

It will ask if you want to Publish repository - click Publish repository button

How to fill this in:

Repository name: desired repository name
Description: any information you want fellow users to know
Keep this code private
Click Create repository button

title: First-time User
text:
1. Download:

Git for Windows
GitHub Desktop


2. Create an Account on GitHub
3. Introduce Yourself to Git (Reference: Chapter 7)

Open R Studio
In the Console, run:

install.packages("usethis")  

library(usethis)  

use_git_config(user.name = "your user name", user.email = "email_address.org")
4. Personal Access Token for HTTPS (Reference: Chapter 9)
This proves that we are a GitHub user, who’s allowed to do whatever we’re asking it to do.

In the Console, run:

usethis::create_github_token()

Your GitHub will pop-up. Ensure that “repo”, “user”, and “workflow” are selected and click “Generate token”. Copy the generated PAT.

gitcreds::gitcreds_set()

Paste the generated PAT

5. Connect to GitHub (Reference: Chapter 11)
Make a Repository on GitHub

Go to GitHub and make sure you’re logged in
Near “Repositories”, click New button
How to fill this in:

Repository template: No template
Repository name: myrepo
Description: Repository for testing my Git/GitHub setup
Public
Initialize this repository with: Add a README file

Click Create repository button
Click <>Code button
Copy the HTTPS address

Clone the Repo to Your Local Computer

In the quadrant where the Console is, click Terminal tab

Make sure that you’re not in a specific directory (ideally ~tmp)

In the Terminal, run:

git clone paste your https address  

cd myrepo  

git remote show origin
Should see something like this:

title: Differences between SAS and R
text:
Sources for this section
SAS Intro 2021| OFE
How to Get Started with SAS: A Beginner’s Guide to SAS Programming | The Open Bracket

The majority of this document is based on coding in R. There are substantial differences between R and SAS that can affect how data is structured and the coding practices used. Below are some major differences in how each software handles data, along with key considerations to keep in mind when transitioning between the two.

Data Structure







SAS
R





Works with rectangular datasets
One dataset at a time


Works with many data structures

Vectors
Lists
Data frames
Tibbles

Columns can contain complex objects (e.g. lists)






Variable Types







SAS
R





Numeric

dates are special kinds of numeric values

Character


Numeric (double)
Integer
Character
Logical
Date-time (class based)






Case Sensitivity







SAS
R





Not case sensitive - can be uppercase, lowercase, or a mixture of both


Case sensitive - will read B and b differently






Naming Conventions







SAS
R





Must start with a letter or underscore ( _ )
Cannot start with a number, contain special characters or blanks


Must start with a letter or number
Cannot start with an underscore ( _ ), contain special characters of blanks






Missing Values







SAS
R





Missing character values are displayed as blanks
Missing numeric values are displayed as periods ( . )


Missing values are displayed as <NA>

Sensitive to how the machine reads







Structure of Command







SAS
R





“statements”
Strung together with semicolon ( ; )
Include “run” at the end of statement
One or more blanks or special characters used to separate words
Can begin and end in any column


“function”
Within a function, strung together with a comma ( , )
Functions are strung together with a “pipe” ( %>% or |> )
No use of special characters
Order matters (e.g. filter, then plot rather than plot, then filter)
Use of parentheses ( )






Comments







SAS
R





/* text /*
* text ;


# text
# text ------------ for section headers (Ctrl + Shift + R)






Environment







SAS
R





Temporary library work
Assign a library libname


Set working directory setwd()
Project-level path .Rproj






Example Code - Import Dataset



SAS





libname data_folder 'C:\Users\SHILL\folder1\subfolder2\sub-subfolder3\stat materials\demo\fox'  
ACCESS=READONLY;run;  
proc datasets lib=data_folder;  
run;  
Data new_name_data;  
Set ohl_data;  
run;



R





setwd("C:/Users/SHILL/folder1/subfolder2/sub-subfolder3/stat materials/demo/fox")  
library(openxlsx)  
new_name_data <- read.xlsx("data_folder/ohl_data.xlsx")


Example Code - Export Dataset



SAS





Proc export  
Data = data_folder.new_name_data  
Outfile = 'C:\Users\SHILL\folder1\subfolder2\sub-subfolder3\stat materials\demo\fox\new_name_data'  
DBMS = dlm;  
Run;



R





library(writexl)  
write_xlsx(new_name_data, "data_folder/new_name_data.xlsx")

title: Navigating through RStudio
text:
Download:

R 4.4.3
RStudio
RStudio is an integrated development environment (aka visualizes what you’re coding).
It is comprised of 4 quadrants:

title: Navigating through RStudio
text:
1. R Script File (.R)

Great for straightforward coding workflows and reusable scripts.
Output is displayed in the console.
Commonly used for:

Data cleaning
Wrangling
Creating functions

title: Navigating through RStudio
text:
2. R Notebook (.Rmd)

Combines code, output, and notes in an interactive format.
Output is displayed in the script file
Useful for:

Exploratory analysis
Learning
Documenting coding process

title: Navigating through RStudio
text:
3. R Markdown (.Rmd)

Designed for creating polished, reproducible reports that combines text, code, and output.
Output is displayed in the script file
Used for:

Sharing analyses (like a report or comms)
Generating HTML/PDF/Word documents


Personally, I use all three of these file types regularly. This will be discussed in more depth in a later section, but in short, I tend to use R Notebooks when I’m exploring a new dataset or initial analyses. R Scripts are useful for creating reusable lists (such as breakpoints used throughout an analysis), writing functions, or even acting as “scrap paper” where I sketch out the structure of a code chunk. Markdown files are ideal for creating outputs 😎 or generating reports with tables and graphs in PDF or Word format.

title: Packages
text:
Packages expand the vocabulary and/or slang, allowing for R to increase their capabilities.
Building a good library (with packages)
Some packages are great, some are redundant, and some aren’t worth having on your roster.

For example: there are at least 3 packages that can import .xlsx files

{openxlsx} - read.xlsx
{xlsx} - read.xlsx
{readxl} - read_excel

There is no right choice but this just highlights that there is different “slang” depending on the package you use and some packages may have other capabilities that you may want.
Both {openxlsx} and {readxl} packages have the capabilities of reading (importing) and writing (exporting) .xlsx files. Whereas, {readxl} package only has the reading capabilities but is part of the {Tidyverse} package ecosystem. This means that if you install {tidyverse} (which is HIGHLY recommended) - it will automatically install all other packages within their ecosystem (including {readxl} ).

Installing a Package
There are 2 main ways you can install a new package:
1. Code in Console
install.packages("tidyverse")
2. Navigate through RStudio interface

In the bottom right quadrant, click Packages tab
Click Install packages
How to fill this in:

Install from: Respository CRAN
Packages: tidyverse
Install to Libraries: C:/Program Files/R/R-4.4.3/library [default]
Install dependencies




Loading a Package
There are 2 main ways you can load a package:
1. Code in Console or Script file

library(tidyverse)

2. Navigate through RStudio interface

In the bottom right quadrant, click Packages tab
Either scroll through the system library or type package in the 🔍search box
Click ☐ for it to appear like

title: Introduction to R
text:
R is a programming language that is known for statistical computing and data visualization. Although, it has a wide range of capabilities including (but not limited to):

Presentations (.pptx)
Reproducible reports (.html, .docx, .pdf)
Microbial analysis (including genomics)
Dashboards

This section will go through:

What are packages and how do we use them
How to Import a dataset
Ways to explore your data
How to manipulate your data
How to export a dataset




Practice alongside the code


If you’d like to follow along, try running each code chunk yourself and experiment with modifying the value to see how the output changes - download the data below!
P.S if you haven’t already - load tidyverse (we’ll need it)


📥 Download Data

title: Export dataset
text:
xlsx

library(writexl)  

write_xlsx(add_rows_data, "data/clean_hockey_data.xlsx") 



csv

write.csv(add_rows_data, "data/clean_hockey_data.csv")



R objects
I want to bring attention to saving R objects, as they can be incredibly useful when working on long-term projects. Saving data as an .xlsx or .csv file can cause you to lose important information from your analysis workflow, such as variable types and other object attributes. Rather than re-running your entire cleaning and wrangling script every time you return to a project, you can save your current progress as an R object and quickly load it back into your environment later.

Save an R object


save(add_rows_data, file = "data/clean_hockey_data.Rds")


Save multiple R objects


save(add_columns_data, add_rows_data, data, file = "data/datafiles.RData")


Save the entire workspace


save.image(file = "data/work_220526.RData")

In all 3 instances, you can load() the file by name and continue your coding adventures from where you last left things rather than starting from the beginning.

load("data/clean_hockey_data.Rds")

title: Practical Guide to Data Management and Analysis
text:
We all have our own ways of managing data and running analyses, and that diversity is part of what makes our team strong. This guide is not meant to suggest that any one method is the “right” way. Rather, it is a collection of practices I’ve found helpful over the years, both as a way to document what I’ve learned and to hold myself accountable to clear, consistent workflows.
In this document, you’ll find practical tips for using statistical software efficiently, avoiding common coding errors, and building workflows that are reproducible, transparent, and easy to share and collaborate on with colleagues.

Size of points

text:
Colour of line

       mapping = aes(x = age, y = circumference)) +   
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "orange") +  
  geom_line(color = "darkgreen")








We can even specify colour by a categorical variable! By applying the colour in mapping(), both geom_point() and geom_line() will be customized.

ggplot(data = Orange,        
       mapping = aes(x = age, y = circumference, color = Tree)) +
  geom_point() +   
  geom_line()








Let’s say we want to specify colours for Tree categories…
We can do this 2 ways:
1. Hard coding

ggplot(data = Orange,        
       mapping = aes(x = age, y = circumference, color = Tree)) + 
  geom_point() +  
  geom_line() +   
  scale_color_manual(     
    values = c(       
      "1" = "#F5276C",      
      "2" = "darkorange",      
      "3" = "blue",       
      "4" = "purple",       
      "5" = "black" 
      )  
    )








2. List

tree_cols <- c( 
  "1" = "#F5276C", 
  "2" = "darkorange", 
  "3" = "blue", 
  "4" = "purple",
  "5" = "black" 
  )  
ggplot(data = Orange, 
       mapping = aes(x = age, y = circumference, color = Tree)) +
  geom_point() +   
  geom_line() +  
  scale_color_manual(values = tree_cols)








Creating a List is a far more reproducible. It allows you to apply that same list to other ggplot() and the code is visually less daunting.
Now that we know how the important components work, let’s simplify the code a bit. The function is smart and knows what to expect in what order so we can remove things!
Let’s remove data, mapping, x, and y …

ggplot(Orange,         
       aes(age, circumference, color = Tree)) +   
  geom_point() +   
  geom_line() +   
  scale_color_manual(values = tree_cols)

title: Recommended Coding Practices
text:
Sources for this section
R 4 Epidemiology (2025). 10 Coding best practices.https://www.r4epi.com/chapters/best_practices/best_practices?utm_source=chatgpt.com9
Coding Best Practices and Guidelines for Better Code | DataCamp
R for Data Science (2023). 6 Workflow: scripts and projects.https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-scripts.html


Key Elements for Coding

Environment: Defining where your files are imported from and exported to is important regardless of the statistical software used. It is highly recommended to work with relative file paths. This will be further discussed in the section Preparing your R Project.

Absolute File Path - as the name suggests, an absolute path points to the same location regardless of the working directory. It usually begins at the computer’s home directory and the follows the same exact directory structure to a file. This can become an issue when sharing code with others, as the same path will not exist on another person’s computer.

C:\Users\SHILL\folder1\subfolder2\sub-subfolder3\stat materials\demo\fox\ohl_data.xlsx

Relative File Path - also self-explanatory, a relative file path is defined in relation to the working directly. This makes sharing code more portable - if someone else copies the project with the same directory structure, the relative paths can still work.

fox\ohl_data.xlsx


Comment Your Code: Providing comments to explain the why behind your code within a script is a great habit! Any text that appears after # on a line is ignored by R, but provides valuable context for future self and colleagues about what the code is doing. You can also make sections withing your code to break your script into more manageable pieces.

# data cleaning ---------------------------------------     
# rename species variables - less confusing  
tidy_random_data <- random_data |>      
  mutate(species = recode(species,
                          "bro" = "broiler",  
                          "cat" = "cattle", 
                          "goa" = "goat"))
To create a header like “data cleaning”, the shortcut is Ctl + Shift + R

Consistent Style:

Case Conventions and Naming - a consistent casing convention should be used across all data frames, variables, and functions. Inconsistent casing can complicate data cleaning and analysis workflows. In addition, avoid spaces, symbols, and special characters. The naming of objects, data frames, functions, and variables should describe what it is. For standardization, snake_case with no capitalization is recommended.

Commas - always put a space after a comma.

title: Best Practices for Spreadsheet Data Organization
text:
Sources for this section
Broman, K.W. & Woo, K.H. (2018). Data Organization in Spreadsheets. The American Statistician, 72(1), 2-10. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2017.1375989
Data Organization in Spreadsheets for Ecologists: Formatting problems


Key Elements for a Project

Raw Spreadsheet: The raw spreadsheet serves as the primary data entry file. It must not contain any calculations, transformations, or derived variables.
Analysis Spreadsheet: The analysis spreadsheet is a secondary version of the raw dataset in which calculations, transformations, and derived variables may be applied.
Data Dictionary: The data dictionary documents all variables and must include variable definitions, permissible values, and variable types.
Cell Formatting and Spacing: Extra spaces within cells can cause errors in data processing and analysis. Avoid introducing leading, trailing, or embedded spaces during data entry. Replace spaces between words with underscores (e.g. max days ➙ max_days).
Case Conventions: A consistent casing convention should be used across all files, variables, and scripts (e.g. snake_case, camelCase, kebab-case, or PascalCase). Inconsistent casing can complicate data cleaning and analysis workflows. For standardization, snake_case with no capitalization is recommended for file names, column names, observations, and code scripts.
Consistency is critical to maintaining data integrity and analytical efficiency. The following practices should be observed:

Categorical Variable Coding: Categorical variables (e.g. yes/no) should be coded consistently across all columns and datasets. Mixing formats such as “Yes”, “yes”, and “1” should be avoided.

When using binary coding (0/1), it is helpful to keep the meaning consistent throughout all datasets (e.g. 0 = No, 1 = Yes).

Missing Value Coding: All cells should contain a value to clearly distinguish true missing data from unintentionally omitted entries. A standardized missing-value code should be used, such as “na” (preferred for R-based workflows) or a “-” . Numeric placeholder (e.g. -999 or 999) is not recommended.
Variable Naming Consistency: When multiple datasets contain equivalent variables, variable names should be identical across all spreadsheets to support seamless data integration.
Subject Identifiers: Unique identifiers used across multiple datasets (e.g. AMU and AMR files) should be consistent in format and value. For example, a subject identifier should not appear as “003” in one file and “CIP003” in another.
Data Layout Across Files: Datasets intended for combination or comparative analysis should follow a consistent structural layout (e.g. all datasets in long format or all in in wide format).
File Naming Conventions: A standardized file-naming convention should be implemented to ensure clarity and long-term usability.

Spaces should be replaced with underscores of hyphens
File names should not include ambiguous labels such as “final version”
The order of naming elements should remain consistent (e.g. group_abattoir 2025_ver2 should not be followed by abattoir_group_2025_ver3).

Date Formatting: Dates stored in a single column should follow ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD). Alternatively, dates may be separated into three columns (YYYY, MM, DD) to facilitate analysis of individual date components (e.g. analysis of month)

title: Functions
text:
Scenario 1 (⭐⭐/5)
It’s that time of year where you perform similar analysis annually. You have separate datasets for E. coli, Salmonella, and Campylobacter and you want to select similar columns from each dataset - but with minor difference, such as an antimicrobial being used for one organism but not another. Rather than repeating most of your code three separate times, you can create a reusable function and apply it across datasets like this:
# create function that specifies relevant columns   
select_amr_columns <- function(df, organism) {
if (organism == "ecoli") { 
  df |>             
    select(  
      isolate_id,
      region,  
      year,   
      month, 
      qtr,  
      sttype,
      final_id_genus, 
      final_id_species, 
      cmic_amc, 
      cmic_amp,  
      cmic_azm, 
      cmic_fox, 
      cmic_cro, 
      cmic_chl, 
      cmic_cip, 
      cmic_gen, 
      cmic_nal,  
      cmic_sss, 
      cmic_tet, 
      cmic_sxt,      
      cmic_tio,  
      cmic_str  
      )        
  } else if (organism == "salm") { 
    df |>      
      select(  
        isolate_id,  
        region,  
        year,   
        month,  
        qtr,   
        sttype,
        final_id_genus, 
        final_id_species,  
        final_id_serotype, 
        cmic_amc,      
        cmic_amp,    
        cmic_azm,    
        cmic_fox,   
        cmic_cro,    
        cmic_chl,    
        cmic_cip,    
        cmic_gen,  
        cmic_nal,  
        cmic_sss, 
        cmic_tet, 
        cmic_sxt, 
        cmic_tio, 
        cmic_str  
        )         
    } else if (organism == "campy") { 
      df |>      
        select(    
          isolate_id, 
          region,    
          year, 
          month, 
          qtr,   
          sttype,
          final_id_genus,
          final_id_species, 
          cmic_gen,    
          cmic_cli,   
          cmic_azm, 
          cmic_ery, 
          cmic_flr,  
          cmic_cip, 
          cmic_nal, 
          cmic_tet,  
          cmic_tel)   
      } else stop("Invalid organism.")    
  }   
# usage of function   
ecoli_amr_data <- select_amr_columns(ecoli_data, "ecoli") salm_amr_data <- select_amr_columns(salm_data, "salm") 
campy_amr_data <- select_amr_columns(ecoli_data, "campy")
Note: There are likely more eloquent ways to write this function (i.e. starts_with() but I initially chose to hard-code the column names. This made it easier to work with a new dataset and explicitly control which variables were included, especially when some columns may no longer be of interest (e.g. cmic_kan).
How it works:

Function Definition

select_amr_columns is the name assigned to the function.

Keyword

function() is telling R that you are creating a new function.

Parameter

df is the input object the function will perform on.
organism is the argument that controls which organism-specific columns should be selected

Function Body

if and else_if are used to check which organism was specified
if (organism == "ecoli") select columns specified in select( ).
else_if (organism == "salm") select columns specified in select( ).
else_if (organism == "campy") select columns specified in select( ).
else stop ("Invalid organisms") generates an error message if a user enters an invalid organism (like "select_amr_columns(ecoli_data, "aeromonas") ).

Usage

ecoli_amr_data is the assigned name for a new output (in this case, a dataframe).
select_amr_columns(ecoli_data, "ecoli") is applying the function to the value ecoli_data , while specifying columns for "ecoli"

title: Functions
text:
Scenario 2 (⭐⭐⭐/5)
Your data may only has MIC variables or you may want to validate the CMIC variables. Rather than repeating most of your code for each MIC variable (there’s quite a few antimicrobials on that panel…), you can create a reusable function and apply it across multiple variables - and even across datasets in the future.
# create function that generates CMIC from MIC  
cmic_expected <- function(df) { 
  mic_cols <- grep("mic_", names(df), value = TRUE)
  for (abx in mic_cols) { 
    x <- str_trim(df[[abx]]) 
    numeric_part <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric( 
      str_extract(x, "[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*")))  
    df[[paste0("cmic_", sub("mic_", "", abx))]] <- dplyr::case_when(     is.na(x) ~ NA_real_, 
                                                                         str_detect(x, "^\\s*(>|>=|≥)") ~ numeric_part * 2,  
                                                                         str_detect(x, "^\\s*(<|<=|≤)") ~ numeric_part,  
                                                                         !is.na(numeric_part) ~ numeric_part,                                                                         
                                                                         TRUE ~ NA_real_                                                                                                                              )       
    }        
  return(df) 
  }  
# usage of function  
ecoli_amr_data <- cmic_expected(ecoli_data)
Note: There is a more efficient way to write this function (i.e. mutate(across())) but I find reading a loop can be easier and I’ve personally used parts of this function for data validation and flagging concerns.
How it works:

Function Definition

cmic_expected is the name assigned to the function.

Keyword

function() is telling R that you are creating a new function.

Parameter

df is the input object the function will perform on.

Function Body

mic_cols <- grep("mic_", names(df), value = TRUE) creates a vector containing all column names that start with "mic_". Setting value = TRUE keeps the actual column name rather than their positions in the dataframe.
for (abx in mic_cols) { } creates a loop that repeats the following instructions for item in the mic_cols vector. In this case, each item repesents an antimicrobial MIC column and is temporarily called abx.
x <- str_trim(df[[abx]]) extracts the current abx column from the dataframe and removes any extra spaces from each observation.
numeric_part <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(str_extract(x, "[0-9]+\.?[0-9]*"))) creates a vector called numeric_part that extracts only the numeric portion from the observations in x.

suppressWarnings( ) silents the warning messages when values cannot be converted numeric values (e.g. abc).

(as.numeric( )) converts the extracted values into a numeric variable type.

str_extract()extracts the numeric portion from each observation in the column.



df[[paste0("cmic_", sub("mic_", "", abx))]] <- dplyr::case_when( ) dynamically creates a new column in the dataframe using the {dplyr} package. The new column name is generated by adding cmic_ to the beginning and removing "mic_" from the original column name (e.g. cmic_mic_amc ➙ cmic_amc). The case_when ( ) applies a series of conversion rules to the observations:

is.na(x) ~ NA_real_, if the orginal value is missing (na), return a missing numeric value (na).
str_detect(x, "^\\s*(>|>=|≥)") ~ numeric_part * 2, if any spaces before text (^\\s*) followed by > OR >= OR ≥ is detected in an observation, return the numeric value multiplied by 2.
str_detect(x, "^\\s*(<|<=|≤)") ~ numeric_part, if any spaces before text (^\\s*) followed by < OR <= OR ≤ is detected in an observation, return the numeric value.
!is.na(numeric_part) ~ numeric_part, if observation already contains a valid numeric value with no inequality symbols, return the numeric value unchanged.
TRUE ~ NA_real_ Any remaining observations that do not match the previous conditions are returned as missing values (na).


Return Statement - return(df) specifies the final output in the function will return.
Usage

ecoli_amr_data is the assigned name for a new output (in this case, a dataframe).
cmic_expected(ecoli_data) is applying the function to the value ecoli_data.

title: Import a dataset
text:
Several types of data can imported to R, including: csv, xlsx, text. In addition, there are two main ways you can import data:
1. Code in Console or Script file

library(readxl)

2. Navigate through RStudio interface
I highly recommend using this method if you are unsure what package to use for the file type. You can always follow the steps below and copy & paste the code preview for your script file.

In the bottom right quadrant, click Files tab
Find the name of file and right-click

Click Import Dataset…

There are a few join functions prefix_join(x, y) :


inner_join() only keeps observations from x that have a matching key in y.

This joins the two datasets together with a shared column players and Players.
If there were more player observations in data, inner_join() would join the observations that match, the remainder would not be included.
If there were more player observations in data, left_join() would join them but those players that are not in new_columns_data would have NA observations in Pregame_drink and Country columns
If there were more player observations in data, right_join() would join them but would only keep those players that are in new_column_data.
If there were more player observations in either data or new_columns_data, full_join() would join them but those players that are not shared in among datasets would have NA observations in Pregame_drink and Country columns.

text:
Sources for this section
An Introduction to R (2026). 7.5 Loops. https://intro2r.com/loops.html
What is a loop | Painless Programming

title: Loops
text:
Structure of a loop

for loop
do this task for a set number of times
for (i in x) {   
  # task 
}

Keyword for ( ): Tells R you want to loop a task for
Parameter i in x: Defines what is being looped. index i is iteratively replaced by each value in the vector x. In simple terms: For each item (i) in x , perform the following…
Result: The loop replaces i with 1 and prints 1, the loop replaces i with 2 and prints 2, the loop replaces i with 3 and prints 3, the loop replaces i with 4 and prints 4, and the loop replaces i with 5 and prints 5.

Note: Loops conventionally use i (short for iteration) but you can use whatever term you like - for (number in 1:5) or even something cheeky like for (KingGeorge in 1:5).
Example

for (i in 1:5) {
  print(i)
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3
[1] 4
[1] 5



Keyword for ( ): Tells R you want to loop a task for
Parameter i in 1:5: Defines what is being looped. index i is iteratively replaced by each value in the vector 1:5. In simple terms: For each item i = 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 in 1:5 , perform the following…
Loop Body

Any instructions that are enclosed in curly braces { }.
print(i) prints i




while loop
do this task until something changes
while (logical condition) {   
  # task
}
Example

i <- 0

while (i <= 4) {
  
  i <- i +1
  
  print(i)
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3
[1] 4
[1] 5


i <- 0 starts at i at 0.

Keyword while ( ): Tells R you want to loop a task while i is within our logical condition.
Parameter i <= 4: Defines what is being looped. index i is iteratively replaced by each value that is equal to or greater than 4. In simple terms: For each item i = 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4, perform the following…
Loop Body

Any instructions that are enclosed in curly braces { }.
i <- i + 1 adds 1 to i value.
print(i) prints i

Outcome:

1 <- 0 + 1

prints(1)

2 <- 1 + 1

prints(2)

3 <- 2 + 1

prints(3)

4 <- 3 + 1

prints(4)

5 <- 4 + 1

prints(5)

stops here because the next i would be 5 which is not <=4

title: Version Control
text:
Sources for this section
What is Version Control?
Let’s Git started | Happy Git and GitHub for the useR

Do you…

Have issues with sharing code with a colleague?
Have multiple versions of code saved because you’re worried about losing historical versions?
Want to work on a project simultaneously with a colleague?

Version control might be useful to you! Imagine a google word doc system for code. It streamlines code development and mitigates lost work and time by tracking changes, enabling multiple people to collaborate simultaneously, identifying conflicting edits, and prevents accidental overwrites.


Basic features

Repository: A centralized database that stores the complete collection of files and folders for a project, along with the revision history.
Commit: A “snapshot” of changes that are tagged and identified - these are changes saved on your local computer.
Push: This saves your commit to the cloud (i.e. visible on your Github.com repository and to other collaborators).

Pull: This grabs any commits that were pushed onto the cloud (i.e. changes made by other collaborators).
Branch: A code that has branched into a separate, parallel version of the main code. This is useful for collaborators to work independently without changing the main code.
Merge: When users combine code edits and integrate changes from on branch into another or into the main code.



Pull Request: Mechanism used to propose, notate, review, and discuss changes in code before they merge into the main code.
Conflict: Ability to identify and resolve conflicting edits or changes among multiple collaborators.


Note: these steps are slightly dramatized in the diagrams. One of the nice features of GitHub is that it guides users through the workflow with prompts for the next steps. For example, after you Commit, GitHub will typically suggest a Push. If it detects changes from another collaborator or a conflict, a Review Pull Request prompt will appear.
This section will go through:

How to set-up as a first user
General use as a on-going user
